interviewQuestions.question: What sections does a good design doc have, and why does the order matter?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The shape I use every time: **problem/context, goals and non-goals, proposed design, alternatives considered, trade-offs and risks**, with an explicit decision ask at the end.

The order isn't arbitrary — each section grounds the next. A reviewer can't judge whether the goals are right without first understanding the problem, and can't judge the proposed design without knowing what it's actually trying to achieve. If I open with the design itself and backfill the problem later, every reviewer has to hold an ungrounded proposal in their head, which is exactly when they miss real issues.

A concrete example: I once reviewed a doc that opened with "we're adding a Redis cache in front of the user service" before saying why. Reviewers spent the first ten comments asking what problem this solved — questions that a two-sentence problem statement up top would have prevented entirely. Rewriting it problem-first cut review time roughly in half because people arrived already agreeing on what needed solving.

I treat the non-goals section as equally load-bearing, not optional — it's what keeps a review from sprawling into scope the doc was never meant to cover.

**Testing:** whether you understand the sections as a reasoning scaffold or just a checklist to fill in.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: How do you write an alternatives section that's actually useful instead of a formality?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I only list options I genuinely considered, and I reject each one with a specific, checkable reason — never a vague "it seemed more complex." A reviewer needs enough detail to disagree with my reasoning if they think I got it wrong; a strawman option gives them nothing to push on.

Concretely, for a recent event-delivery design, I wrote: "Option A — Kafka topic per event type — rejected: operational overhead of standing up a new system outweighs the benefit at our current ~500 events/sec." That's falsifiable — someone who thinks Kafka's overhead is overstated can say so directly, citing our actual ops load. Compare that to "Kafka felt heavier," which nobody can argue with because there's no claim in it to test.

The test I apply to my own draft: could someone who disagrees with my choice write a rebuttal to a specific sentence in this section? If the section is vague enough that a rebuttal would have to start by asking me what I meant, I haven't done the work yet.

I also make sure the chosen option isn't obviously the only one that got real treatment — if two options get three sentences and the winner gets a page, that's a defend-the-decision doc wearing an inform-the-decision doc's clothes.

**Testing:** whether you can produce falsifiable reasoning under pressure, versus post-hoc justification for a decision you'd already made.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Alternatives

interviewQuestions.question: You circulated a design doc a week ago and got zero substantive feedback. What do you do?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Silence on a design doc almost never means "everyone agrees" — it usually means the ask was diffuse or the doc wasn't clearly someone's job to review. I'd fix the process before assuming the design is fine.

First move: check whether I actually named specific reviewers with a specific ask, or just posted "sharing for visibility" to a wide channel. The second gets ignored because everyone assumes someone else will look at it. I'd re-send to two or three named people — "@name, need your sign-off on the consistency model in section 4 specifically, by Thursday" — which converts a diffuse ask into an unambiguous one with an owner.

Second, I'd check whether the doc actually states a decision deadline and what approval means. If it doesn't, I add that near the top: "Decision needed by Friday; approve if you're comfortable with the trade-off in section 4." Open-ended review windows are how docs die quietly.

Third, if it's a genuinely important decision, I'd book 20 minutes with the key reviewers, having asked them beforehand to read it first, and use the meeting to resolve open threads and get a verbal decision rather than a first read-through live.

What I wouldn't do is treat silence as approval and start building — that's how you find out three weeks later that a reviewer had a real objection they never got around to typing up.

**Testing:** whether you diagnose silence as a process problem you can fix, or just proceed and hope.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Getting review

interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide whether a change actually needs a full design doc, versus a quick message to the team?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My heuristic is reversibility and blast radius, not team size or how long the work will take. I ask: if this decision turns out wrong, how expensive is it to undo, and who gets hurt while it's wrong?

A config tweak, an internal refactor with no external API surface, or a change I can revert with one commit doesn't need alternatives sections and a sign-off deadline — a three-line Slack message with the reasoning is proportionate, and demanding more just trains people to skim docs. On the other end: a new public API, a schema migration on a table other services depend on, or anything touching auth or payments gets the full treatment, because reversing a bad decision there means a migration project of its own, not a revert.

I've seen both failure modes cost real time. Over-formalizing trivial changes is subtle — nobody complains loudly, but reviewers learn most docs don't matter, so the one time it's the risky change, it gets the same shallow skim as everything else. Under-formalizing a risky change is more visible — it shows up as an incident or a costly migration a few weeks later, exactly the failure a design doc exists to prevent.

So in practice: I size the document to the cost of being wrong, and I say that reasoning out loud when I skip the full template, so it reads as a judgment call rather than laziness.

**Testing:** whether you can calibrate process weight to actual risk instead of applying one template uniformly or skipping it uniformly.
